body:
If you can make an example data sample available, I could try to determine what is going on.

A few observations:

- The t-tuple behavior that you are seeing (t = 614) suggests that substrings of 614 symbols repeat at least 35 times, which suggests that this source outputs long sets of repeated strings. This may be made worse by a data formatting problem, but the assessed entropy is probably going to be quite low.
- You may be seeing a problem in the LRS test because the longest repeated substring is evidently quite large, and it turns out that the computational task associated with the LRS test scales with the length of this string.
- You examples all seem to use the C++ tool, not the Python tool. If you are actually using the Python tool, you shouldn't. It is hundreds of times slower than the C++ version, it was an implementation of an outdated version of the (then) draft SP 800-90B standard, and it has a bunch of bugs that aren't fixed.

Thank you for the reply.

I'm in fact using the C++ tool, I just use Python in order to run the tests, so it was my mistake.

[RawRandom_1220MB.zip](https://github.com/usnistgov/SP800-90B_EntropyAssessment/files/6539747/RawRandom_1220MB.zip)

> If you can make an example data sample available, I could try to determine what is going on.

> A few observations:
> 
>     * The t-tuple behavior that you are seeing (t = 614) suggests that substrings of 614 symbols repeat at least 35 times, which suggests that this source outputs long sets of repeated strings. This may be made worse by a data formatting problem, but the assessed entropy is probably going to be quite low.

>     * You may be seeing a problem in the LRS test because the longest repeated substring is evidently quite large, and it turns out that the computational task associated with the LRS test scales with the length of this string.
> 
>     * You examples all seem to use the C++ tool, not the Python tool. If you are actually using the Python tool, you shouldn't. It is hundreds of times slower than the C++ version, it was an implementation of an outdated version of the (then) draft SP 800-90B standard, and it has a bunch of bugs that aren't fixed.

The longest repeated substring in that dataset is 656384 symbols long, and the t value for the (literal) data is 167. As such, the tool needs to estimate the W-tuple collision entropy for every tuple length between these two values. That will take a while to perform the calculation, but it should eventually work out.

This is an incredibly long repeated substring for a data set of this size, and this suggests that the assessed entropy is going to be very very low.

Here are the literal results. I'm not sure there's much use in performing the full calculation.

```

Literal t-Tuple Estimate: p_u = 0.9225963965587568
Literal LRS Estimate: u = 168
Literal LRS Estimate: v = 656384

Literal LRS Estimate: p_u = 0.99996638712268315
Literal t-Tuple Estimate: min entropy = 0.11622843729515714
Literal LRS Estimate: min entropy = 4.849394643012541e-05
```

I'll summarize: the tool seems to be working fine, but this specific estimator detects defects in the provided data that are so large that it takes the tool quite a while to properly calculate just how low the estimate ought to be.
